# Distances of Moon, Sun and stars (parallax) (`astronomical_distances`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs round_earth_size, trigonometry; helped by telescope, keplers_laws, pendulum_clock
- Core idea: Distances in the sky are found like a surveyor's: observe the same body from two places a known distance apart and measure how far it shifts against the background (parallax). The Moon is about 60 Earth radii away (384,000 km), found already in antiquity. The Sun is about 150 million km away, some 400 times further than the Moon and 109 Earth diameters wide; this needed telescopes and observers on different continents (Mars in 1672, Venus crossing the Sun in 1761 and 1769). Kepler's third law then gives all other planets. The nearest stars are a few hundred thousand times further than the Sun; their yearly shift as the Earth moves is under one second of arc and was first measured in 1838.
- Pitfalls:
  - Quoting the modern figures without any method; the numbers alone convince nobody
  - Using Aristarchus' half-moon method, which is sound geometry but gave a Sun 20 times too near
  - Expecting to see stellar parallax with early instruments; its absence was the main argument against Copernicus
- History: greece: c. 270 BC Aristarchus: Sun about 19 times further than the Moon; c. 140 BC Hipparchus: Moon at about 60 Earth radii; Ptolemy's solar distance of about 1200 Earth radii stays standard for 1500 years; islamic: 9th–11th c. – al-Farghani and al-Battani refine the Ptolemaic distances; europe: 1672 Cassini and Richer, parallax of Mars: Sun about 140 million km; 1761 and 1769 transits of Venus observed worldwide; 1838 Bessel, parallax of 61 Cygni; americas: 1912 – Henrietta Leavitt's period-luminosity law for variable stars opens distances beyond parallax
- Read:
  - Albert Van Helden, Measuring the Universe: Cosmic Dimensions from Aristarchus to Halley (1985)
  - Alan W. Hirshfeld, Parallax: The Race to Measure the Cosmos (2001)
